title: Setting Terms: Siempre Que, Con Tal de Que, A Condición de Que

sections.title: A condition that must be met
sections.content: You know *con tal de que* "as long as" from B1 Unit 21 and *siempre que* "provided that" from B2 Unit 7. They introduce a condition that must be met before the main clause holds, and the verb that follows is always in the subjunctive: the condition looks ahead and is not yet a fact. After a present or future main verb you use the present subjunctive; after a conditional or past main verb you use the imperfect subjunctive. New here is *a condición de que* "on condition that", a more formal way to set terms. Do not confuse the condition with the other meaning of *siempre que* from B2 Unit 7: with the indicative it means "every time that" (*Siempre que viaja, llama a su madre*).

sections.title: Ways to set a condition
rows: as long as (I can accept it if…)
con tal de / a condición de + infinitive
same subject in both clauses, as in B2 Unit 4

items.spanish: Firmaremos el contrato siempre que nos den más tiempo.
items.english: We will sign the contract provided that they give us more time.

items.spanish: Acepto el trabajo con tal de que me dejen trabajar desde casa.
items.english: I accept the job as long as they let me work from home.

items.spanish: El banco dará el crédito a condición de que presentemos todos los documentos.
items.english: The bank will give the loan on condition that we present all the documents.

items.spanish: Iría a cualquier parte con tal de viajar con ustedes.
items.english: I would go anywhere as long as I travel with you.

items.spanish: Dijeron que firmarían siempre que les diéramos más tiempo.
items.english: They said they would sign provided that we gave them more time.

sections.content: Never put the future or the conditional after these conjunctions: say *siempre que respeten el plazo*, not *siempre que respetarán el plazo*, even when the main verb is in the future.
